newsitem.title: USA: Washington wheat weekly ratings drop seen anomaly.
newsitem.headline: Washington wheat weekly ratings drop seen anomaly.

text.p: A change in the reporting base for winter wheat condition ratings in Washington, the second largest U.S. winter wheat producing state, exaggerated the state's and the overall U.S. weekly ratings fall Monday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, analysts said.

"A lot of that change just reflected we had a lot better coverage with our survey this week than the previous week. It is probably more of that than a huge change in the way the conditions are," an official at the Washington Agricultural Statistics Service said.
Analysts said they had been puzzled by the large decline.

Non-irrigated winter wheat in Washington was rated one percent excellent, 44 percent good, 46 percent fair and nine percent poor the week ended Sunday. A week earlier it had been rated 17 percent excellent, 66 percent good, 14 percent fair and three percent poor.
Irrigated winter wheat was rated 93 percent good and seven percent fair, versus 15 percent excellent, 78 percent good, seven percent fair a week earlier.

Washington was the second largest winter wheat producing state last year with output of 164.5 million bushels, second only to Kansas which produced 255.2 million, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture figures.
USDA reported Monday that 46 percent of U.S. winter wheat was rated good or excellent, versus 63 percent a week earlier.

While Washington's reporting base, which took into account more data last week than the previous week, partly accounted for the fall in overall U.S. winter wheat crop ratings, harsh spring weather in the Plains states also contributed.
The report reflected the impact of a cold snap that damaged winter wheat in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, USDA said.
